item.title: The Problem With Happiness
item.description:
Happiness

The Problem With Happiness

Why happy people can’t agree on how they got there.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • Perspective is power: True lasting happiness begins with shifting your mindset.
  • Mastery fosters meaning: Engaging deeply in lifelong, challenging pursuits helps develop personal growth.
  • Connection provides purpose: Shared community creates essential frameworks for long-term fulfillment.

If you’ve read our most recent posts, you may be concerned that this is turning into a blog about boomerangs. It’s not, we promise.* This is a blog about moral psychology and well-being. At the World Boomerang Championships this summer, Ed learned a few things from the best throwers in the world, who generally enjoyed high levels of psychological well-being to go along with their gorgeous boomerangs.

In such a diverse group (11 countries represented, ages 13 to 70), it was odd to see uniformity, even around a basic trait like happiness. So, as an annoying scientist does, Ed went around asking everyone, “What is the key to lasting happiness?” Speaking in their native languages, 15 competitors responded.

This wasn’t terribly scientific. But it did surface one of the problems with happiness: Everyone wants it, there are decades of research about it, but there is no consensus on how to get there. Case in point: Ask 15 people, and you'll get 15 answers that don't reduce to one. Here's what they told us, in no particular order:

Throw boomerangs

This obviously should be in the latest research.

Take charge of your perspective

Be present, be positive, and be grateful. “The simplest or most direct way to be happy is to find the right perspective” (Florin, Germany; a remarkable 15-year-old).

Loofy, who lives in France and is from “a country called Planet Earth,” finds happiness in the moment. “Always remember the past, never have regrets, and live the present as intensely as possible. Follow the true rule of punk, which is ‘No Future.’ Never think about the future. Make the present magnificent and the future will be magnificent.” Punk, existentialist, optimist. That’s Loofy.

Challenge yourself and forget yourself

Engage with the world. Embrace challenges. Find flow. Seek mastery. Create. Play.

“Do something that is difficult enough… maybe easy to start, but difficult to master. And then you have something to do for the rest of your life. I started this boomerang thing when I was 13. And this is over 40 years ago, and I still feel like a beginner on most days” (Günther, Germany).

Transcendent human connection

Forgetting ourselves creates space for human connection. Junji from Japan believes in the importance of seeing ourselves as parts of continually changing, dynamic networks of personal relationships.

For others, it is a combination of family, friendship, and community. “For me, happiness is seeing my children flourishing” (Jérôme, France). “What is the key to happiness? It’s love. To be truly loved and to genuinely love” (Adam, UK).

We also connect through culture, food, tradition, and even farming. Indian thrower Arun finds joy in festivals like Pongal, celebrated together with friends and family. “We perform prayers to the sun, asking for blessings of health, prosperity, and abundant harvests so that food will be available for everyone.”

Agency

David, a recently retired Australian thrower, reflected on personal freedom as key to happiness. For him, freedom from the need to work pointed to endless possibilities.

For Günther, it was about freedom from judgment. “If you do not watch other people too much, and you try not to feel judged, then it's easier to be happy.” Wagner from Brazil reflected that “it is much better to assume your mistakes. It is much better to assume your responsibilities because that makes you grow.” Maybe happiness comes from judging ourselves on our own terms rather than ceding that power to others.

Fitness

Physical well-being is another path to freedom. For example, good health enables Arun to farm, which is a source of happiness in his life. For him, farming and celebrating were on interwoven strands of happiness. As the French thrower and revolutionary designer Sébastien noted, “I think the key to long-term happiness is family stability, having hobbies—like boomerangs—and maintaining good physical health.”

Existentialism

“The key to happiness is realizing you’re utterly miserable” (Matt, Australia). Crikey.

This may seem counterintuitive, but underneath this bleakness lie profound existentialist ideas. He elaborated that “Happiness is a job that must come from within. It’s an inner job essentially to achieve a modicum of happiness in view of the tragic impermanence of life.”

Many others saw a role for struggle in their philosophies of happiness as well. “It is precisely the small traumas of life that forge our character” (Wagner). It may surprise you to learn that the existentialists in our little sample were among the happiest of this happy tribe. You can find it in their philosophies if you squint just right; their acceptance of tragedy makes the experience of happiness more visible, just as a birthday candle stands out in a dark room. Loofy’s rejection of the future means that this moment is everything.

More than one thrower was candid about the personal struggles they have faced, including depression, childhood trauma, and personal health struggles. Perhaps these struggles do more than offer the backdrop that makes the candles of happiness more visible. Perhaps they make the candles more precious. And when those candles are needed, these folks go out of their way to light a few themselves.

To be clear, no one is suggesting trauma as a pathway to happiness. Trauma causes real and lasting suffering. Far too many people struggle with it throughout their lives.

Nonsense

“Always have enough nonsense in your head” (Klaus, Germany).

Clearly, there is no one key to happiness. There are many proven ways to unlock that door. These boomerang champions arrived at the same end from radically different directions. The takeaway? Our paths will always look different, and comparing your journey to another's is a dead end. We think you need to choose your own way and maybe keep a little bit of nonsense in your head for good measure!

*That said, the world could use another English-language boomerang blog. Our favorite is from France.

item.title: AI and the Threat of Cognitive Inhibition
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and the Threat of Cognitive Inhibition

What if AI changes our propensity to think?

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • AI may actively compete with human thought by taking over cognitive work.
  • Repeated AI use may also change our willingness to think for ourselves.
  • High affinity is not the same as healthy function, for hemoglobin or cognition.
Source: Image by mostafa meraji from Pixabay

There is something I find fascinating about carbon monoxide. The gas is molecularly simple (one carbon and one oxygen), colorless, and odorless. Yet once it enters the blood, it takes on a "life" of its own by binding to hemoglobin with more than 200 times the affinity of oxygen. And interestingly, carbon monoxide poisoning is generally associated with a cherry-red or pink appearance, which is an almost perverse contradiction where this toxicity can carry a color we associate with health and vitality.

It sounds like something from Gabriel García Márquez, where magical prose combines with bitter almonds, poison, and a touch of unrequited love. There is something beautiful and deceptive about the physiology, which may be why this idea has resonated with me since my days as a firefighter and paramedic. Oxygen is what the body needs, yet carbon monoxide is simply better at the binding site.

My contention is that there's a simple yet powerful idea here. High affinity does not necessarily mean that something is good for a person or system. Lately, I have been wondering if this has something to teach us about artificial intelligence.

When AI Competes With Thought

Let's start with the idea of cognitive work. Do I do it—think about it or write it? Or do I hand it off to an LLM and get the answer in seconds? The result may often be similar, but the workflow isn't.

In this context, AI seems to have an extraordinary affinity for "doing the work" for us. AI is fast and even fun. And in a biological sense, this begins to look a little like a type of competitive inhibition because AI can occupy that cognitive space where "effortful thought" once was our "cognitive oxygen." Simply put, AI competes with our brains.

It's important to recognize that this doesn't mean that AI always diminishes cognition. I have often had the opposite experience and I expect that you have, too. My idea of iterative intelligence came from those exchanges where an answer from AI becomes the start (not end) of a power dynamic.

Something Else May Be Happening

Carbon monoxide gives us another interesting perspective. Its effect is broader than just binding tightly to hemoglobin. Once CO is bound, it changes the structure of the hemoglobin molecule, making bound oxygen harder to release to tissues. The interaction of CO with hemoglobin affects the behavior of the larger system.

Could it be possible that our interactions with AI begin to influence how we think? If answers are always there at our fingertips, maybe uncertainty itself finds a new and higher level of intolerance? And if well-crafted solutions arrive at the touch of a button, maybe our human cognitive path begins to feel less critical or even important.

And yes, I'm using biology here as an analogy. I'm not suggesting some hidden receptor deep in our neuroanatomy. Still, this possibility fascinates me because the effect on us could be new—on some fundamental level. It's no longer the "quid pro quo" relationship of handing a task to a machine and getting the answer back. Noncompetitive inhibition describes how the broader and larger function of a system is altered by the battle for a receptor site. I wonder whether there's a cognitive correlate to that idea worth exploring?

AI can compete with our act of thinking. But repeated interactions may do something more subtle. It may begin to change our propensity to engage in "effortful thought" in the first place. A type of cognitive inhibition.

What AI Does With Us

Maybe this is part of what makes AI "feel" different from earlier tech. A calculator adds a group of numbers, and search finds information for me to review. Both are more transactional than iterative. But an LLM can enter our thinking while the thought itself is still taking shape.

And that can happen before I have decided what I was trying to say in the first place.

Of course, that can be enormously useful. There are moments when the AI's coherence sharpens and expands our own thinking. But there are also moments when I wonder if AI's answer arrives just too soon. The thought looks finished, yet my cognitive task remains somewhat jilted.

Much of the discussion around AI has focused on what the technology does FOR us. I'm becoming more interested in what happens when AI begins doing things WITH us, participating in thought while it is still emerging and influencing what comes next.

The Part We May Not See

Cognition adapts to the environment (think neuroplasticity). And AI is, without a doubt, becoming part of that environment. I don't know if repeated use produces anything that deserves the name "noncompetitive cognitive inhibition," but I think the question is worth asking.

What if AI does more than compete with thought and begins to change our propensity to engage it?

Here's my hyperbolic take-away. CO gives you that rosie look of oxygenation. And AI gives you that look of cognitive authority. But all may not be as it seems. The biology reminds us that the thing that binds most readily is not always the thing the system needs. And that's something worth thinking about.
